label: Halloween

what_happens.title: What happens on Halloween
goals: Kids walk with grown-ups and say trick or treat
Some things look spooky but are pretend
what_happens.parentSkill: Walk the trick-or-treat route in daylight first so your child sees the decorations without the dark.

who_is_there.title: Who I will see
goals: Masks and costumes are people underneath
who_is_there.parentSkill: Show your child how a mask works by putting one on and taking it off a few times.

what_i_do.title: What I do on Halloween
goals: Stay with the grown-up and carry a light
Say trick or treat and thank you
Let a grown-up check the treats
what_i_do.parentSkill: Agree the rules: hold hands near roads, only lit houses, treats checked at home.

if_scared.title: If it feels too spooky
goals: Feeling scared on Halloween is normal
Calm tools: hold a hand, skip a house, go home early
if_scared.parentSkill: Never laugh at the fear. Say: 'That looks scary. It's pretend, and we can skip it.'

rehearsal.title: Let's practise Halloween
goals: Try on the costume and practise walking in it
Practise trick or treat and thank you at home
Practise putting on and taking off a mask
rehearsal.parentSkill: Do a home trick-or-treat: knock on a bedroom door, say the words, get a treat.

steps: Choose and try on a costume
Wait until it gets dark in the evening
Walk with a grown-up and a flashlight or glow stick
Knock or ring at houses with lights on and say, trick or treat
Say thank you and take a treat
See decorations, some silly and some spooky
Go home, check the treats with a grown-up and share the stories
sensory: spooky sounds and laughter from decorations
a bag that gets heavier with candy
honestyNotes: Some decorations and costumes are designed to look scary, and a child may be frightened; never say 'there is nothing to be scared of'. Masks are people underneath. Children can skip houses, leave early or stay home and hand out candy instead. Treats are checked by a grown-up first.

fallbackAnswer: No. Monsters, ghosts and skeletons on Halloween are costumes and decorations.
Every mask has a person underneath.
Feeling scared is okay. You can hold a hand, skip a house or go home.
[[GROWNUP]] is with you the whole time.

questionButtons.text: Why do we go out in the dark?
fallbackAnswer: Halloween happens in the evening so the pumpkins and lights glow.
We bring a flashlight so we can see.
Yes, [[GROWNUP]] walks with you the whole time.
We stay together and hold hands near roads.
Neighbours who want to share treats.
We only visit houses with the lights on, and [[GROWNUP]] stays with you.

questionButtons.text: When can I eat the candy?
fallbackAnswer: After a grown-up checks it at home.
Then you can choose a few.
Anything you like: an animal, a hero, a food or something you invent.
You can be silly or spooky.
Masks are part of the costume and make dressing up fun.
You can ask someone to lift theirs, and you will see a person.
Knock or ring, then say, trick or treat.
When you get a treat, say thank you.

questionButtons.text: What if I can't eat some candy?
fallbackAnswer: We can swap it for something you can have.
Some houses give toys or stickers instead.

questionButtons.text: Am I too old for trick-or-treating?
fallbackAnswer: Lots of older kids still dress up and go out.
You can also help little kids or hand out treats.

techniques.label: A daylight walk
techniques.how: Walk the route in daylight first to see the decorations.

techniques.label: Mask peek-a-boo
techniques.how: Put a mask on and off at home to show it is a person.

techniques.label: Skipping a house
techniques.how: Let your child skip any house that feels too spooky.

techniques.label: A flashlight or glow stick
techniques.how: Let your child carry their own light.

techniques.label: Holding hands
techniques.how: Hold hands near roads and in crowds.

techniques.label: Checking treats
techniques.how: Check treats together at home before eating.

techniques.label: Home trick-or-treat
techniques.how: Practise knocking and saying the words at home.

techniques.label: Handing out treats
techniques.how: Stay home and hand out treats if going out feels too much.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

ritual: Knock, trick or treat, thank you

sentences.text: Soon it will be Halloween.
Halloween is a night when people dress up in costumes.
First [[CHILD]] puts on a costume, maybe a dragon, a superhero or a pumpkin.
Then, when it gets dark, everyone walks with a grown-up and a flashlight.
Before bed, here is a story about a little bat called Benny.
In Bat Valley, there was a night called Glow Night.
Everyone dressed up, and Benny was a fluffy cloud.
First Benny's mother gave him a little glowing lantern.
Then they flew to the houses with lights on.
Knock, knock, said Benny, glow and treat!
A kind owl gave him a juicy berry.
Thank you, said Benny.
Some houses had silly paper spiders, and some had funny pumpkins.
Benny went home with a bag full of berries and a big smile.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
Next they knock on doors with the lights on and say, trick or treat.
The people give a treat, and everyone says, thank you.
There are decorations, some funny and some spooky, and they are all pretend.
Last, it is home time, and a grown-up checks the treats.
[[CHILD]] can choose which houses to visit and which to skip.

The dark can feel big, and decorations can make strange sounds.
Some masks look scary, with big teeth or glowing eyes.
Feeling scared is normal, even for big kids.
All the spooky things are pretend, made of plastic, paper or cloth.
In the story, Benny the bat got scared.
A house had a skeleton that rattled and laughed, ha ha ha.
Benny's wings shook.
Mama did not say, that is not scary.
Mama said, that looks scary, and it is a plastic toy that moves.
Do you want to skip it, she asked.
Benny nodded, and they flew away from that house.
Benny took a slow breath and held Mama's wing.
At the next house, a smiling pumpkin glowed orange.
That one is friendly, said Benny.
Worried and brave can happen at the same time.

Halloween comes from old autumn festivals where people dressed up and lit lanterns at the end of harvest.
Today it is mostly about costumes, decorations and sharing treats with neighbours.
Houses with a porch light on are usually the ones taking part.
Safety rules, like staying on sidewalks and carrying a light, matter on dark streets.
[[CHILD]] can plan a route with [[GROWNUP]] using a map.
Some people decorate to be as scary as possible, like a haunted house; that is a choice, and skipping it is fine.
Neighbours who hand out candy are part of a community tradition.
Some kids have allergies, so some houses offer non-food treats, often marked with a teal pumpkin.
Groups of older kids may trick-or-treat together with a grown-up nearby.
[[CHILD]] can say hi to neighbours they have not met before.
Reflective tape or glow sticks on costumes make kids visible to drivers.
Masks can block side vision, so face paint can be safer.
Checking treats is about spotting open wrappers or allergens, not something to worry about.
Sorting and trading candy afterwards is half the fun.
[[CHILD]] can agree a candy plan with [[GROWNUP]]: how much tonight, how much later.
Being scared by something you know is fake still triggers the body's alarm, which is why haunted houses work.
Some people enjoy that feeling, and some do not, and both are fine.
Jump scares are designed to surprise; knowing that helps.
If [[CHILD]] sees something upsetting, talking about it at home and how it was made helps the brain file it as pretend.
[[CHILD]] can be in charge of choosing the route.
Testing the costume ahead of time catches problems like tripping hems or masks that block vision.
Charging flashlights and packing a bag for treats saves time.
Planning a route with known neighbours makes the night feel safer.
Agreeing what to do if anyone gets separated is a smart family rule.
[[CHILD]] can help decorate the front door for the kids who visit.
